rationale: One more self-contained source item for the remaining budget: the log-store interface duties and the contracts the library relies on beyond index and term. The interface documents a freedom that the replication and snapshot paths actively depend on - stored batches may leave gaps, and Raft uses a gap as the signal that logs before a restored snapshot are discontinuous - with an opt-in interface for stores that cannot tolerate gaps. The same file documents the barrier contract and explicitly disclaims the log timestamp as coordination input, which corrects a reading that operational timestamps could stand in for ordering.

investigations.question: Which duties does the captured LogStore interface impose on an implementation, and which of them does Raft rely on for correctness rather than for storage alone?
investigations.hypothesis: Beyond storing and retrieving entries, the interface grants a freedom that the library depends on: a stored batch may be non-contiguous with previous logs, and Raft uses that gap to resynchronise followers after a snapshot restore, offering the MonotonicLogStore opt-in for implementations that cannot tolerate gaps. A store that cannot tolerate gaps but does not declare the opt-in would silently change what Raft believes about discontinuity, which is the kind of consumer/producer mismatch worth stating. Timestamps in the log are explicitly operational only, and the barrier type carries a stronger completion contract than a no-op.
investigations.discriminator: Compare the interface documentation with the call sites that consume FirstIndex, LastIndex, StoreLogs and the barrier type: a defect on the library side would need a call site that assumes a property the interface does not promise, or a store property the library never reads. For a store implementation the question is whether it can tolerate gaps and, if not, whether it declares IsMonotonic; the captured in-memory store stores by index and does not implement the opt-in, so it relies on the documented gap freedom.

knowledge.statement: The LogStore interface promises FirstIndex and LastIndex returning 0 when there are no entries, requires GetLog/StoreLog/DeleteRange (inclusive range), and explicitly allows StoreLogs to leave a gap between previous logs and the stored batch. Raft relies on that gap as the signal that logs before a restored snapshot are discontinuous, and offers MonotonicLogStore.IsMonotonic for stores that cannot tolerate gaps, in which case Raft removes all previous logs after a snapshot restore instead of relying on the gap. The captured in-memory store indexes entered logs by index and does not implement the opt-in, so it relies on the documented freedom.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to any LogStore implementation used with the captured revision; the gap-reliance affects the paths that resynchronise followers and restore snapshots, and the opt-in is only consulted where old logs are removed.

knowledge.statement: Two documented contracts bound what the log types mean. A LogBarrier exists to ensure all preceding operations have been applied to the FSM and only returns once the FSM manager acknowledges it, so it is not equivalent to a committed no-op. A log entry's AppendedAt is operational information only: it is not used for coordination or as part of the replication protocol, followers may observe a future timestamp due to clock skew, and the leader is not required to persist before delivering to followers. The oldest-log helper tolerates truncation racing with its read by retrying until the first index is stable or a hard error is returned.
knowledge.conditions: Applies to the captured revision's barrier handling, to any component that reads AppendedAt (for example age metrics), and to the oldest-log metric helper.

interpretations.rationale: The duties are documented where they are consumed, and the two surprising ones are freedoms rather than obligations. FirstIndex and LastIndex are specified to return 0 when there are no entries, which is what the snapshot and replication code relies on when it decides whether a prefix is available (for example the last-index helper returning the maximum of log and snapshot index). StoreLogs is explicitly permitted to store a batch that is not contiguous with previous logs, and the library uses that gap to mark the discontinuity created by a snapshot restore; stores that cannot tolerate gaps must opt in through MonotonicLogStore.IsMonotonic, after which Raft removes all previous logs instead of relying on the gap. The captured in-memory store inserts entries by index and does not implement the opt-in, so it takes the gap branch - consistent with the fork in the install path that chooses between removing all old logs and compacting. The barrier type carries its own documented contract: it exists so that callers can be sure preceding operations reached the FSM, and it resolves only when the FSM manager acknowledges it, which is stronger than a committed no-op and matches the ordering observed earlier in the apply path. Finally, AppendedAt is disclaimed as a coordination input: it is operational information, followers may see a future timestamp from clock skew, and the leader is not required to persist before delivering log entries, so nothing may treat it as an ordering or freshness signal - a reading worth recording because age metrics are derived from it. No defect is claimed; the one consumer/producer mismatch that would matter belongs to a store implementation that needs monotonicity without declaring it, which is outside the captured snapshot.
counterevidence: The only mismatch found is on the implementation side (a store needing monotonicity without declaring it), and the captured in-memory store correctly takes the gap branch instead of claiming monotonicity.

The barrier contract explains why a Barrier is a stronger synchronisation point than a no-op, which is consistent with the apply-path ordering established separately in this run rather than contradicting it.
limitations: Source-only; no custom store was written and no gap-dependent resynchronisation was executed for this question.
Third-party stores shipped outside this snapshot were not inspected.
The call-site survey covers the paths read in this run (replication, snapshot restore, install, oldest-log metrics), not every use of the store interfaces.
